passage_title: Freezing of Droplets Containing Mineral Powders
passage:
Water droplets can stay liquid well below 0 °C. A droplet freezes when it contains a surface that can start ice growth, so the temperature at which a droplet freezes depends on what is suspended in it. Researchers studied four powdered minerals, labeled Powder 1 through Powder 4, that had been ground to the same particle size range.

Study 1. Each powder was stirred into pure water to give a suspension of known concentration, in milligrams of powder per liter of water (mg/L). Droplets of 1 μL each were placed on a chilled metal stage coated with oil and cooled at 1 °C per minute while a camera recorded the temperature at which each droplet turned to ice. Two hundred droplets were run at each combination of powder and concentration. The median freezing temperature is the temperature by which half of the droplets had frozen. Droplets of powder-free water were run in the same way and are plotted at 0 mg/L. The results are shown in Figure 1.

Study 2. Suspensions of each powder at 10 mg/L were divided in two. One half was left untreated; the other half was held at 95 °C for 30 min and then returned to room temperature. Droplets were made from each half and cooled as in Study 1, and the percentage of droplets that had frozen by the time the stage reached −20 °C was recorded. The results are shown in Figure 2.

explanation: Along the Powder 2 curve the successive medians are −28, −26, −24, −22, −14 and −12 °C. The rise from 6 mg/L to 8 mg/L is 8 °C, whereas the rise from 0 mg/L to 2 mg/L, from 2 mg/L to 4 mg/L and from 8 mg/L to 10 mg/L is 2 °C in each case.

passage_title: Freezing of Droplets Containing Mineral Powders
passage:
Water droplets can stay liquid well below 0 °C. A droplet freezes when it contains a surface that can start ice growth, so the temperature at which a droplet freezes depends on what is suspended in it. Researchers studied four powdered minerals, labeled Powder 1 through Powder 4, that had been ground to the same particle size range.

Study 1. Each powder was stirred into pure water to give a suspension of known concentration, in milligrams of powder per liter of water (mg/L). Droplets of 1 μL each were placed on a chilled metal stage coated with oil and cooled at 1 °C per minute while a camera recorded the temperature at which each droplet turned to ice. Two hundred droplets were run at each combination of powder and concentration. The median freezing temperature is the temperature by which half of the droplets had frozen. Droplets of powder-free water were run in the same way and are plotted at 0 mg/L. The results are shown in Figure 1.

Study 2. Suspensions of each powder at 10 mg/L were divided in two. One half was left untreated; the other half was held at 95 °C for 30 min and then returned to room temperature. Droplets were made from each half and cooled as in Study 1, and the percentage of droplets that had frozen by the time the stage reached −20 °C was recorded. The results are shown in Figure 2.

prompt: Suppose that droplets containing Powder 1 had also been tested at a concentration of 5 mg/L. Based on Figure 1, the median freezing temperature of those droplets would most likely have been closest to:
explanation: On the Powder 1 curve the median is −18 °C at 4 mg/L and −16 °C at 6 mg/L, so a value midway between them, about −17 °C, is expected at 5 mg/L. −18 °C and −16 °C are the two plotted values themselves, taken by reading the nearer point instead of interpolating, and −15 °C interpolates between the 8 mg/L and 10 mg/L points instead.
